utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There's a matter I'd seek to raise in the absence of the witness in relation to this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In relation to this witness. Then General Radinovic, I'm sorry, but I have to ask you again to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the Chamber appreciates your patience. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are in open session again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Being the last day in all likelihood of the Defence case, there are some matters of disclosure in relation to rebuttal that I must attend to out of court. I'd be grateful for an indication as to when I might revisit the issue of the fifth videotape in relation to the evidence of Richard Gray.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that we'll not spend much time any more on General Radinovic, and perhaps we could deal with it then right afterwards. That would be my suggestion. Yes. General Radinovic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And yesterday I reminded you, and I'm doing the same again today, reminding you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. We were about to hear what questions Judge El Mahdi would have for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] General, I would like to ask you two or three questions. The first of them in a way picks up on a question that was asked of you by Honourable Judge Nieto-Navia. It concerns the relationship between the JNA and the forces of Republika Srpska. I would like to take you back to your report, paragraph 2. Do you have your copy? Yes, please. If you can follow me, in the English version it's paragraph 2. It's probably the same in your language. I'm quoting in English: [In English] "The former Yugoslavia conducted in the period 1991-1995" - et je voudrais precise en fait les dates que vous avez vous-meme mentionnees - "Was an internal thus, a civil war and not an international conflict." [Interpretation] You added, and I quote: [In English] "Conducted within one international recognised nation-state. In this war, the forces Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. involved in the conflict were the forces of one and the same nation-state and of its army JNA against the forces and movement of secessions." [Interpretation] End of quote. I would like now to refer you to your conclusions, number 7, which is on page 175, also in the English version, where you mention, and I quote: [In English]" -- Yugoslavia continued to support and aid VRS in an expression of national solidarity which could have been done by any army in the world but none of the forms of this assistance was violating the principle of non-interference of Yugoslavia in this internal conflict in BiH." [Interpretation] End of quote. You answered yesterday in response to a question by Judge Nieto-Navia that the only link between the two armies, if I can call them like that, is that the Yugoslav Federation paid out pensions to the families of the fighting men of the Republika Srpska army. My first question would be this: You, as a military man, do you believe that the nature of the conflict has an impact on the applicable law in the context of the accusations -- of the charges levelled against General Galic, in terms of military terms? The acts allegedly committed by General Galic, would they be of a different nature, depending on how we qualify the conflict? What is your position on this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, in the second paragraph of my report you quoted the English version, and unfortunately it was not translated well. You said the war was waged with one internationally recognised state, whereas I wrote it was waged within one international recognised state. Forces within that state were fighting each other, whereas you read out the translation as reading that war was waged with one internationally recognised state. That's not what I wrote. In my view, the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina is an internal war waged between forces between that state. Three ethnic communities had a conflict within their ethnic rights, depending on their different perceptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me. My question is two-pronged. First of all, in military terms, the laws of war, the laws of warfare, in the context of the charges levelled against General Galic - I'm not speaking in general terms. I'm speaking about this context - would the rules of armed conflict change depending on how you qualify this conflict, as an international conflict or a national conflict? And is this why you specified in your report - and this is my second question - how were you able to arrive at this conclusion that you stated in your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the first part of your question, would the nature of the war affect the application of the law on warfare?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the applicable rules. You as a military man, you are surely aware of rules that apply to an international conflict, as opposed to a national conflict. Do you, as a military expert, believe that the rules and provisions that apply would change depending on the nature of the conflict; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I am not a legal expert, but I know the demands and requirements of international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You as a general.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that. I know that. The nature of the war that was waged in Bosnia and Herzegovina indisputably affects also the nature of responsibility and liability of everyone in that war, including General Galic, precisely because the rules of international law that apply to every conflict, including this one, acquire a different meaning versus a regular war, where you know exactly where the front lines are, where the troops are, where the civilians are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So my second question, if you allow me: What was your basis for the conclusion that this particular conflict was a national one?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I relied, first of all, on the relevant documents, on books written by people whom I held in high esteem as people knowledgeable about military matters, and on my knowledge gained over several decades about war as the subject of military science. If we talk about this war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it happened within Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state. Of course it started before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you give me a couple of references, perhaps, of the material you relied upon.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, General Rose wrote in his book that the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina was a civil war. You must believe me when I say that I have great respect for what General Rose has done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you read General Rose's book in English?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the Serbian translation, and the Defence team has the book in English, in both languages, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you as a military expert, do you believe that the conclusions and the interpretations of events stated by General Rose reflect the real situation, are a genuine reflection of reality? Has this been proven in your view in this work, and do you believe in his impartiality?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First let me finish what -- about what I have read about this war and its nature. So I read the book by Pierre-Marie Gallois, one of the most prominent military theoreticians. The book's title --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the title.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention it here but I mentioned it in other cases testifying before this Tribunal. He wrote in detail about the nature of the war, and he concluded in no uncertain terms that it was a civil war. Professor Gavro Perazic, professor of military law in Podgorica, a retired colonel who used to be a professor at the military academy of military law also wrote a book where he very clearly emphasised that it was an internal war. Professor Smiga Avramov wrote a book entitled, "the Anti-heroic War of the West against Yugoslavia," wrote that it was an internal war within Yugoslavia with all the attributes of religious wars which are the bloodiest of all. From the beginning of the war to date, many scientific gatherings have been held in Yugoslavia discussing the subject of war in the territory of Yugoslavia, and these seminars and meetings concluded that it was a civil war. Based on all the material that I have studied, I have absolutely no reason not to accept this conclusion because my own findings from my own research and studies about this war are identical because the citizens of one state, Bosnia and Herzegovina, were involved, namely there are three ethnic communities each of which in their own way perceived their own rights within that state. When Yugoslavia was broken up, all these three ethnic communities clashed over their rights. With the intervention of the International Community, which was not efficient, which tried to impose peace but failed, and instead let this internal conflict happen. Each of these ethnic communities had their own army, their strategy, their doctrine, and within the framework of those doctrines they waged this war. We can analyse this very broadly and at length, but in essence this is an internal civil war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. But will you please look at paragraph 7 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, but the interpreters, as the transcript says, missed the title of one of the books that were used by this expert. It's a book by Pierre-Marie Gallois. Would you please find out from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you're referring to General Radinovic rather than General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] Yes. It's the end of the trial. Yes, in fact. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please have a look at paragraph 7 of your conclusions, where you say: [In English] "The Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina continued to support and aid --"

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just find that place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: " -- VRS in an expression of national solidarity." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. [Interpretation] Are you following me, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did you mean exactly when you said -- when you wrote that there was continuous support, that there was continued support and aid from the Yugoslavia army, that is to say, from the Federal army for the VRS in an expression of national solidarity? Could you elaborate on that? What did you mean when you wrote this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I meant what is stated here. There is no doubt as to the meaning of this. The Army of Republika Srpska is the army of part of the Serbian people. The Army of Yugoslavia was the army of the Serbian people living in Serbia and Montenegro. As far as national identity is concerned, these two armies are absolutely identical. It assisted the Army of Republika Srpska in all legitimate respects, with regard to everything that was legitimate. It made efforts to attain just objectives, objectives not forbidden by international agreements and conventions. The Army of Yugoslavia did not prevent officers and non-commissioned officers from its composition who were born in Bosnia and Herzegovina or in Republika Srpska. They didn't prevent them from leaving the Army of Yugoslavia and from fighting, because that was the patriotic duty of every officer. Every officer has to be ready to defend his people if they are threatened. So I'm not arguing for or against that war, but it's a well-known fact that that people was involved in a war and every officer, a non-commissioned officer had the patriotic duty of participating in that war. The Army of Yugoslavia considered that every honourable officer had the duty of going to fight for his people. Furthermore, the Army of Yugoslavia took care in material and social terms of officers, that is to say, of their families who remained in Yugoslavia, and thus made -- didn't distinguish between the families of officers and non-commissioned officers who remained within Yugoslavia. Furthermore, the Army of Yugoslavia educated high-ranking officials of the Army of Republika Srpska for the functions that were necessary. The Army of Yugoslavia helped certain special industries to be reanimated in Bosnia and Herzegovina through which this army could be supplied. The Army of Yugoslavia helped within the framework of the entire state programme for humanitarian aid. And furthermore, the Army of Yugoslavia, in terms of doctrine, provided support, informed of all the rules and instructions that were necessary for the organisation of that army. So in other words, it did everything that a friendly country would do. Our country did this, or rather, our army. So this is the form of assistance that I was thinking of. I also know that material was obtained, purchases were made. I don't know whether this was cash or whether there were some sort of other arrangements, but purchases were made, certain material resources were purchased in order to supply that army. For example, certain spare parts, parts for servicing equipment, repairing equipment that was a bit worn out, et cetera. And there were certain assemblies too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll move on to another subject. It's paragraph 36 in your conclusions. And you conclude that Sarajevo was not a city either under siege or a city that had been subject to a blockade. Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Having affirmed that - and I quote - "[In English] -- Under siege or a city under blockade," - vous avez dit - "blockade pertained to the Muslim part or more precisely to the part under Muslim control. Blockade referred to the Muslim army." [Interpretation] My first question is: You used the definition or, rather, the definitions of siege and blockade. Are you using these definitions or is this a military definition that could be quite different from the legal definition of the terms "siege" and "blockade", because you mentioned a siege and a blockade, and in the first part of the paragraph you said that Sarajevo was neither under siege or under blockade.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, I was referring to the terms used in the indictment. In the indictment they mention the terms "siege" and "blockade." And in the explanation of this conclusion, I was thinking of what a blockade meant in military terms, what the term "blockade" meant in military terms, not in legal terms, because I'm not a lawyer so I'm not in a position to know what meaning this might contain, legally speaking. But the term "blockade" in military doctrine is used for military action around cities, around settled, inhabited places. These are very delicate combat operations, military operation, because cities are the most resistent points, the toughest points when it's a matter of conquering them militarily. And the doctrine that prevailed, that was part of the doctrine of the JNA, which is a doctrine that was adopted by all three sides in the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, states that cities should not be conquered but that cities should be blocked. They shouldn't be taken over; they should be blocked. And a blockade imposed on a city, according to military doctrine, the military doctrine that I'm referring to here and the military doctrine about which I am writing, entails controlling the main roads, the main points, the main features, the entrances to and the exits out of the city for military forces. So it refers to military forces. A city in which military forces are based must be blocked in such a way so as these forces can't leave the city or new forces can't enter the city because this would disrupt the balance of military forces and the side imposing the blockade on the city could find itself in an interior position. So the blockade of Sarajevo - and when I refer to the blockade of Sarajevo, I'm referring to the blockade of the forces of the 1st Corps within Sarajevo, the attempt to prevent them from going to Igman or Ozren and joining up with forces in the direction of Visoko, the direction of Olovo or Igman, because in such a case the war in the Sarajevo theatre would have been a lost cause for the SRK, for the Army of Republika Srpska, and the war in Bosnia would have been a war lost by Republika Srpska. So it was in that sense that I was referring to actions to cause a blockade and not to a blockade in order to suffocate the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But my problem is that initially you denied that the city was under siege or that there was a blockade of the city, and then you carried on saying that the blockade was imposed on the part that was under Muslim control, and this is where I understood or misunderstood something. After having denied that the city was under siege or that the city had been -- that there was a blockade of the city, then you said that nevertheless there was a part of the city that had been blockaded. And this is what is causing me certain difficulties. If I understood you correctly, you said that there was a blockade but you are making a distinction between a siege and a blockade by referring to legal notions contained in the terms of siege or blockade. So were you referring to legal notions or exclusively to military notions? Initially you said that Sarajevo was under blockade, or at least the Muslim part was under a blockade.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are a few distinctions I would like to make here. First of all, in the second sentence of paragraph 36 of my conclusions it doesn't say that the Muslim part of the city was under blockade but that the blockade pertained to the Muslim army, the BH army. So it refers to the military aspect alone. And secondly, and the previous part of my answer refers to this, I want to say that a blockade as a military action is a legitimate action. From the point of view of military doctrine, it's entirely legitimate as an action. What is important is how it is carried out. A blockade is a legitimate action. What is important in this case is whether all other measures taken are legitimate. So this is a general doctrine that I would like you to take into account when I refer to a blockade here. And now, was Sarajevo in fact under a blockade or were the military forces in Sarajevo under a blockade? I don't think they were. Or in fact, this is not just my opinion. I have documents, and I have referred to these documents, some of them have been shown here, and these Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. documents clearly show that not even the military forces of the 1st Corps of the BH army in Sarajevo were under blockade. This was not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're introducing a nuance. You are -- when you say that there was a blockade -- you said that there was a blockade, but now you say that even with respect -- in regard of the military forces, there was no blockade.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this conclusion, this follows from the entire report, my entire analysis. But I have just exposed in a few words what was explained. The army of the 1st Corps -- the troops of the 1st Corps of the BH army wasn't under a blockade for the simple fact -- and documents bear this out, and chief of staff of the 1st Corps Nedzad Ajnadzic wrote about this in his book, "The Defence of Sarajevo," I think that's what it's called. He says that the 1st Corps as of May of 1993, from each brigade in Sarajevo would occasionally take a battalion out to Igman and they would be trained there for future combat activity, in order to join up with forces on the outside front, on the external front. Furthermore, there is an entire series of documents from the commander of the 1st Corps, General Karavelic, who testified before this Tribunal. There is a document in which he orders the command of the Dobrinja Brigade to take a battalion to Igman via the airport. General Rose also mentioned the fact that Sarajevo wasn't under blockade. Throughout the war the airport in Sarajevo was open. International delegations would arrive there. There was -- there were a lot of institutions, international institutions and organisations in Sarajevo, humanitarian routes functioned, the blue routes were open. It was possible to leave Sarajevo and it was possible to enter Sarajevo. Naturally, under control because it was war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I will move on to another subject. Could you please tell me, with regard to the objectives, the targets that you marked on the map -- do you remember the map of the city?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you marked at least 1.500 military targets on that map. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I mentioned 220, but I said that there were -- 1.500 or over 1.500 targets every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well. But my question is: Did these targets exist towards the end of 1992? The number didn't increase, or did it gradually increase with the passage of time? At the end of 1992, how many military objectives were there? Your map and the objectives, the targets that you marked there, do they represent the targets at the end of the war or, rather, at the beginning of the war? Because I'll clarify this: You referred to documents, for example, the date of which was 1993 or 1994. So I suppose - and I think that this is one of the questions that the Prosecution wanted to put to you. I didn't follow your answer, and I would like to know whether the way that these military targets were presented, the ones you referred to on the map, did these targets exist throughout the conflict, from the very beginning of the conflict to the end of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The map I provided and the list of targets with the list of documents should be viewed within the context with reference to the central map where all the brigades of the warring sides in the Sarajevo theatre were marked. And also, with reference to the map in the western part of the front, that map refers to the position of the 102nd Motorised Brigade of the 1st Corps of the BH army. On the big map I presented the front, I represented the front, I represented the way it changed, and I represented the main changes on that front. I mentioned that in 1992 the front changed at Doglodi. At that time General Galic and his corps improved that part of the front, improved the tactical position by taking Otes and in December, but in the second half of December, the 1st Corps took Zuc, Vis, Brijesce Brdo, and right up to Rajlovac and Vogosca and significantly improved their tactical position in that way. Apart from those changes there were no other changes throughout the wartime period. So all the brigades that were in Sarajevo in the second half of 1992 remained there until the end of the war. The only thing that changed was their names, and the brigades swelled up, so instead of one there were two zones of responsibility. The number of targets did not change, and not even their location changed. They remained where I marked them. They could have moved to a very insignificant extent because those zones of responsibility of the brigades and these zones were fixed zones throughout the wartime period. They were always present; they were always there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you for your answer. My last question has to do with the structure of the Republika Srpska army. You make a distinction between the higher ranks who were former officers of the Federation and paramilitary forces that formed the lower ranks. In your opinion, did military discipline reign or did it not reign? Was it in force in the strict sense throughout the wartime period in the Republika Srpska army, and in particular in the Romanija Corps? Was there discipline?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this question relates to the influence of the character of war and to how international rules regulating war are applied. As far as the top levels of the army are concerned, as far as the main institutions that are part of the command system are concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, General, but I'm referring to military discipline above all. Did the chain of command go from the top levels down to the simple soldiers? Was this -- did this function smoothly? But you also mentioned the existence of paramilitary forces. You said that there was quite a bit of -- there was a significant lack of discipline within the corps. And as an expert, would you have judged -- would you have said that this army corps was a disciplined corps that followed military rules?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this corps was a disciplined corps. It did respect the discipline that was established by military rules. But there were certain shortcomings, which I mentioned in the documents, and General Galic took efforts, made efforts to deal with resistance that appeared in certain paramilitary units and also to deal with the lack of discipline on the part of certain brigade commanders who were under the direct influence of local politicians, politicians who kept interfering with the system of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. [In English] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have the following question for you: You have answered questions in relation to strategic important hills around the city. I do not know whether I could follow all the hills you mentioned, but I would like to specifically ask you whether the higher grounds in the north-east and eastern part of the city in the direction of Hresa or Faletici or Mrkovici, were they of any strategic importance?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were. And in that part, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had the advantage with regard to the BH army 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes it's difficult to find the geographic names you mentioned. Could you tell us where in your report you described that in this respect the SRK had an advantage. I see that the matter is dealt with, I would say, in the spatial and geographic determinants. That's, at least, where I try to find it. Could you guide me and tell me where in the paragraphs 77 to 80 you are referring to these SRK positions on higher grounds that gave an advantage.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. Let me find my bearings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it Ozren that you are referring to or ...?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's part of the Sarajevo area from the Trebevic slopes to Hresa and Ozren. That's the northern part. It's above Mrkovici and Radava.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there was an advantage to the SRK, where exactly do I find that?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I can be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 157 after footnote 91. "Only the SRK had the advantage from the part of the front up to Radava."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that I left this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sometimes I would mention certain villages that are known in my mind, and perhaps you are referring to other villages in the same area. So I'm just trying to compare where I find it. You said in 157.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is 157, second sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you say Zlatiste to Radava, that's the same area I just referred to, that is the same area, that is Hresa and Faletici and Mrkovici.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even closer from Kneginjac, to Faletici, across Hresa, to Radava. That is the semi-circle south, south-east, and north-east.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was just trying to compare my points of orientation with yours, and you take different ones but you're referring to the same area. My next question would be: You have told us that you studied many books on the character of the conflict and that you concluded that the character of the conflict was a internal conflict rather than an international conflict, a civil war. Did you study the case law of this Tribunal in this respect as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not only with reference to this case but also when I prepared to testify in other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But even in cases where you perhaps did not testify --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You might have noticed that in some decision the Tribunal concluded that the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, whether in whole or in part, was an international conflict. I take it that you disagree with those conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't agree with that conclusion. And I have offered my arguments against it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it on the basis of, did you say, the Tribunal has wrongly established facts or is it on the basis that you say that on the facts that are established they have drawn the wrong legal conclusions out of that? Is it -- do you disagree mainly on the basis of the facts underlying the conclusion of the Tribunal or is it on the basis of the conclusions drawn on the basis of the established facts?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did not dare to criticise the conclusions of the Tribunal here. I criticised implicitly, rather, the experts who had prepared the background material that gave rise to such conclusions by the Tribunal. I studied Gow and some other authors who I can't remember. But in the Tadic case, the Talic case, in the Krstic case, Kunarac, Dokmanovic, Krajisnik, all the cases that I could study, all the material that I could lay my hands on, I studied. The part which qualifies the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina as an international conflict is the part I disagree with. I believe that I am right, and I have profound arguments to support my view, but it is up to the Tribunal to decide, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I do understand you well that you say the experts that have provided the facts underlying the conclusion of the Tribunal, some changes of the Tribunal, that the conflict was of an international character, those experts have not presented the facts in a correct way or perhaps even wrongly?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. General Radinovic, let me first ask the parties whether on the basis of the questions asked by the Bench there's any need to put further questions to you. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. First of all, I apologise. We still don't have the title of that book that I wanted to get a moment ago when I interrupted Honourable Judge El Mahdi. I did not mention the name of General Galic but the author Gallois, who was by the interpreters and I said that the interpreters had said that they missed the title of this book. I did not get an answer to my question so I'm asking it of the witness again so that we have it on record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you again give us the title of the book you just referred to, that is, the title of the book by Mr. Gallois, Pierre Gallois, if I understood you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Pierre-Marie Gallois wrote a book called "The Blood of Petrol Bosna," that is, at least, the Serbian translation. I don't know the French title, the original title.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Mr. President, I have three or four questions. The first two have to do with the questions asked by Honourable Judge El Mahdi.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you were asked questions about by the assistance of the JNA extended in this conflict, how it assisted and so on and so forth. My question is as follows: Could you tell us, in terms of distribution of weapons by the JNA, relative to the barracks in Sarajevo during the events from the beginning of the war, namely, do you know whether these weapons were distributed, if at all, to one side or the weapons were distributed, if at all, to several parties, to several sides?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, that goes beyond the scope of questions put by the Bench and could have properly been raised in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me, counsel, that you are entitled to ask several questions, but this does go beyond the scope of the questions I asked and the answers the general gave, so you're entitled to ask a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me that you are right. Thank you for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you have, General, an answer to my question? In your knowledge, what can you tell us about the assistance of the JNA, for instance, in terms of the distribution of weapons by the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps a matter of clarification. With respect to what Judge El Mahdi said, it's unclear whether or not the objection was sustain or denied with respect to this question, which again has been put to the witness, at least with respect to the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi intended to deny the question but at the same time said that it went beyond the questions. So I take it that only to a limited extent questions will be allowed in this respect. So could you tell us anything about the distribution, General Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Weapons were partly stored in depots within the framework of the strategic reserves of Bosnia-Herzegovina that were founded long before the war, and each side looted the depots that were on its own territory. As for the weapons that were in use in units, we know that on the 4th of May, 1992 the decision was made to withdraw the JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina within 15 days. This term was very short, and it was absolutely impossible to withdraw the JNA within that term, so military property and resources were looted and confiscated. Parts of these resources, parts of the weaponry of the units that were within the composition of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps remained within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, whereas some part of the weaponry was taken over by the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Muslim army in the course of lootings of depots and robberies. So parts of the weaponry were kept and parts were taken away. That's the brief answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. But have you found during your studies a document that would establish an interparty agreement on the distribution of weapons?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the question -- we have established that it was beyond what was asked by Judge El Mahdi. Apart from that, the matter is dealt with in the report. So therefore, please move to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'll move on to a different subject, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, in response to a question by Honourable Judge El Mahdi you answered that the army, despite this blockade, the BH army still managed to get out of what you call the interior circle and to transfer its battalions. You mentioned specifically the territory of the airport which gave breathing space to the city. Here is my question: Did you see more than one document that would allow you to assert this, that is, the existence of movement of troops from inside to the outside?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That was answered by the witness in response to the question from Judge El Mahdi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it was an introductory question because what I really wanted to do, with the Court's leave, is that we put on the ELMO a document that we have found - and we'll give you a number soon - which illustrates this type of situation from which we can see that it was on documentary basis that the general was able to conclude this, and it has to do with the BH army. I think this goes to the very essence of our proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Concentrating on the basis of the source of the answer, rather than to question --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then briefly you're allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Would you kindly put this on the ELMO. So let's put this one on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could either get a copy or an indication of what the document is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We have all the documents for distribution, with the kind assistance of all involved, together with translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, I believe you now have the document in front of you. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My first question: Is it one of the documents of whose existence you just told us?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a document that the staff of the Supreme Command sends to the command of the 1st Corps ordering the 1st Corps to take certain action, certain movement from Sarajevo towards Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to squander the time I have at my disposal, but during your study and research, were you able to examine other documents of the same nature and perhaps the same contents as this one?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found documents where the plan is made for the use of tunnels below the airport and ordering the brigade commander in whose area of responsibility the tunnels are, specifying the precise timetable of entrances and exits from the tunnel, and it has to do with movements of troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, let's look at the second part of the paragraph 2, which says "crossing from."

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "During the execution of the task, prevent self-removal"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, the sentence that begins with "prelaz", "crossing."

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The next sentence after the one you're in.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see. The second sentence says: "Effect the crossing of the runway by units and by parts of units reducing to the minimum the risk and probability of conflict with UNPROFOR."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Are we talking about days or nights? Because this document talks about night-time crossings. So if troops are crossing the airport, would that be a legitimate objective?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would certainly represent a legitimate target for the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My penultimate question: You told us briefly something about discipline in an army corps, specifically relative to the forces that are named paramilitary forces. Here is my question: Were you able to find - and if yes, in what measure - documents from which we could clearly see that General Galic made all efforts possible to control the situation, in terms of discipline, precisely in order to avoid problems such as disorganised elements, unwarranted opening of fire, et cetera? So if you found such documents, what could you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was preparing to write my report, I found a wealth of documents, starting from October, the first documents were dated in October and the General Galic assumed command of the 7th of September, as we know. From the beginning of his term in this position, General Galic was resolutely fighting illegitimate behaviour, conduct by all such units that were arriving to the front line, and improper conduct by some of his subordinate commanders. He was also resolutely combatting the unwarranted interference by local authorities - and here we have references to illegal transfers of oil, robberies, threats by his own units and his own command, that they would settle accounts with him, the replacement of Major Dunjic, then the situation on the front when he sent a group of officers headed by Marcetic, chief of staff, and another officer, when he established a forward group on the front line in order to establish control over such undisciplined units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood you correctly and if we proceed from the principle that before General Galic assumed command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You first said one question, and then you said the last question, and then the last question became the penultimate question. Is this your last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my very last question, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I wasn't really translated. I'm talking about the principle that -- the situation was a bedlam really, a powder keg. The situation was like sitting on a powder keg, was a bedlam, very chaotic, a bedlam really.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So in view of that situation, how much time - just give us an order of magnitude - how much time did it take a responsible person in the military --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, that question has characteristics of being misleading. It also mischaracterises the testimony and the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin, to start with, you are creating a picture first, a picture in which the witness only has to fill in one element, and the picture is yours. That is leading. Could you please put a question without first creating the picture --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ask a question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Taking into account, General, what you just told us about the situation concerning discipline and from your experience as a military man, how much time would it take a corps commander to restore order to the functioning of units in his command? In other words, if everything was organised to perfection, it would take two days. And if not, how much time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. That's clearly a hypothetical question. It calls for speculation. There's no factual foundation in the question that would allow the witness to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond, Mr. President? This is absolutely not a hypothetical question for the reason that the general was able to examine an important number of documents, that he was able to see this, he was able to establish the level of organisation that existed, and he knows as an expert - and his report shows it very well - he knows very well what stages are necessary in such a reorganisation. He should know whether General Galic was able to restore order within two days or more. And that is -- it is in this capacity that I'm asking him the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would have no question -- no objection if he put the question in the way he just phrased it to the Chamber with respect to this accused and this situation. In terms of referring to a corps commander -- if the question was simply rephrased, we would have no objection, if it's relating to the specific facts of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please rephrase the question and refrain from introducing all kind of elements which are not in evidence and that are [Previous interpretation continues] ... Hear the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I begin taking into account your statement? Because it has to do with the answer he just gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- let me ask the question to you. In the circumstances you described, how much time it would need for General Galic to restore a disturbed order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under normal circumstances - and I'm now talking about normal circumstances - the corps commander takes 15 to 30 days to assume his duties. So much time is given to him for the transition of duties, to read all the reports, to inspect his units, and to finish by saying "I have now assumed my new position." In the situation when General Galic became corps commander and in the operative situation, which I described in my testimony and in my expert report, it is absolutely beyond reason to imagine that General Galic could have restored order in the operative situation in less than two months. From the end of 1992 to the beginning of 1993 he was busy restoring order and certain deficiencies continued to cause failures throughout the war in the command system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your answer. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you for this question. That was my last question. But before we finish, we just wanted to say that there are documents that we want to tender from the bar table in the traditional way. I'm saying this so that it's clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis, is it clear what documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, before that, the Prosecution had two questions arising from either the Bench or from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I should have given you an opportunity. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, with respect to an answer given by you to a question from Judge El Mahdi, you said that the Army of Yugoslavia did not prevent Bosnian Serbs from returning to Bosnia to perform their patriotic duty, fighting to defend their people. Did Bosnian Serbs in fact return to Bosnia in order to do just that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying that they returned to do that, but if they returned for only that reason I don't know. It was not the subject of my particular study and it's not a proper question for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You -- a few moments ago in response to a question from the Defence, you indicated that the -- that Marcetic established a forward group. Do you know the name of the group that was established?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Marcetic did not establish a forward group. He established a forward command post on the orders of the corps commander as his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know where that forward command post --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have an objection, a delayed one. We believe that again we are witnessing what we called yesterday a fishing expedition and we don't want to fall into the -- run into the same difficulties again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, on page 29, line 22 you will see reference to - at least in the English transcript - or lines 21 and 22 Marcetic, chief of staff, and another officer when he "established a forward group on the front line in order to establish control over such undisciplined units." That was in response to a question from the Defence. My question simply was: If there was a name of this forward group. The witness has now told us it was a forward command post, and the only remaining question I would put to the witness, if I'm permitted to do so, is where on the front line that forward command post was located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please put that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you've just told us that Marcetic established a forward command post on the orders of the corps commander. Where on the front line was this forward command post?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forward command post was located in the barracks of the Butile installation. It is the large depot in the western part of the Sarajevo region. The forward command post was sometimes also located on the Nisic elevation, in Ilidza, in Trnovo. Forward command posts are set up as required. Whenever the need arises, a forward command post is sent out. General Galic also formed a group of officers headed by Kosovac, who was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Yes. I am sorry for the interpreters that I interrupted. Until now you were only asked where it was located. You've have answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then General Radinovic, this concludes your testimony in this court, and I should perhaps add to you "in this case." We'd like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague and having answered all questions from parties and from the Bench. And before I ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom, I'd like to say a few words to you in private session. Could we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I would like to invite the parties to see whether we can deal with the exhibits introduced through the witness Radinovic or from the bench -- from the -- yes, from the bar table, yes. I'm still not a trained common lawyer. To do that at a later stage if the parties would agree so that in order -- I do not know that I was aware that the expert witness to come would not be available at the beginning of next week, but let's see how far we come. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note that I haven't been given an opportunity to respond. I don't seek it. I think there are more important matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. It's a matter -- it's a matter that doesn't need any decision, I would say, at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, we heard that Mr. Piletta-Zanin was complaining about what happened. We cannot change that any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. And I won't put on the record the Prosecution position in relation to what he said. I should note that the transcript as to what was said before the break in relation to my interjection is incomplete. What I in fact said was "this should stop, Mr. President. This should stop." Mr. President, moving on, there is the matter of the videotape, and I note in relation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- To the remainder of the day, that earlier this week you said that there might be some further sitting time this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It has not been arranged for, as a matter of fact. But we could see -- I'm a bit surprised by the fact that the next expert witness is not available in the beginning of next week any more. But there were quite a lot of problems to continue this afternoon, but we still could see whether we could gain an hour somewhere. But the Chamber -- at least, I have some other arrangements as well this afternoon, made only after we decided that we'd try not to rush and push the matter. So therefore, we'll have to perhaps first ask the expert witness when she could come. But let's first start and see how far we come.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The response of the Defence is obviously that we agree with your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is, to postpone the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I haven't heard the Prosecution's response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution would have no objection to that, Mr. President. But perhaps it might be helpful in order to prepare our response to the various documents if the Defence perhaps later today or this evening could indicate their specific position with respect to the various categories of documents which have been dealt with by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's not quite clear to me what you asked them, but perfectly out of court you'll be able to communicate with them what you'd like them to inform you about. Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort the next witness into the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not the only one, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, therefore, you'll -- you'll be -- get more information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this witness will be cross-examined by Mr. Stamp, who's on his way down at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We hadn't anticipated we would start straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mrs. Radovanovic. You -- always my first question is whether you hear me in a language you understand. You seemed not to do a minute ago but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Radovanovic, before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration of which the text will be handed out to you now by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Ms. Radovanovic.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you, first of all, introduce yourself to us. Could you tell us where you were born, when, and what you are by profession.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Svetlana Radovanovic. I was born in 1949 in Sombor. I graduated from the Faculty of Philosophy, and I obtained my MA and Ph.D. From the Faculty of Geography. At the moment I am the chief of the department for demography and I work at the university in Belgrade in the Faculty of Geography.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Radovanovic, at the Defence's request you submitted a report, submitted it to the court on the 29th of January, 2003; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you stand by everything that you wrote in your report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But there are certain amendments I would like to make. When I compared the English and Serbian version, I realised that certain errors were made. On page 4 of the English text, the translation is not correct. You don't say -- it shouldn't say "incompetent," it should say "incomplete." On page 12 of the English version, there is another error. In the Serbian translation I got table 2 and in the third column there is no date. That date is contained in the English translation. Perhaps I used more severe terms because I was sure that a translation couldn't contain such an error. It's an official translation. And on page 19 of the English text, instead of the number "6" -- instead of the number "600," the number should be "699."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is that all, Mrs. Radovanovic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Ms. Radovanovic. I couldn't follow you. You mentioned page 4, and you said that a word -- but I don't know where is the word. Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll tell you immediately. I'll try and do that right away. In the Serbian version, under the title "Main conclusions," that's page 4 of the English version, item A, it says "all the data sources used for the analysis --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I already -- I already found it. I already found it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says "incomplete," but the English translation says "incompetent."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: And the second issue refers to page -- the second issue refers to page --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on page 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any problem with the audio?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I think that the witness has problems with the headphones. I just wanted the witness to be assisted. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: And then you made the reference to page 12 of the Serb -- Serbian version. But I would like you to repeat that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 12 of the English version. And that's page 7 in the Serbian version. There is a table which says "Representation of all the phenomenas represented in the PDS sample."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That table consists of three columns. In the third column, where it says "PDS 1994," in the translation it didn't include this date that you have in the English text, which says "10/9/92 until 30/9/94." In the Serbian version, it's on page 03032066. That date isn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: You mean the date which says "01/01/92-30/09/94" in the English text is not in the original?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. That date, the 1st of January, 1992 to the 30th of September, 1994, that date is there, but there are three columns in the table. The first table says "all," and then you have the date, the 1st of January, 1992 up until the 30th of September, 1994. And then in the Serbian version you don't have anything but in the English version you have the date, the 10th of September, 1992 to the 10th of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: In fact, I was checking both versions, and I think that they are identical. I don't see the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To clarify the matter, may I intervene? Just to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I checked that with the witness. The version that the witness is referring to is not the version of her report. It's the translated version that was provided to her by the Tribunal's service. It's the version of the -- of Tabeau's report. In the translation of Tabeau's report - and I verified this myself - in table 4, this table was not completely translated, and that's where the error occurred. In the translated document, the document translated by the Tribunal, and the expert worked on the Serbian version of this document, in the translation you don't have this element which is in the report submitted by the expert Ewa Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Okay. It's a different issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Radovanovic, on page 1 of your report, you provided a summary of the results to which your main conclusions were added.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The first question I would like to ask you is: The statistical analysis in undefined parts of the six Sarajevo municipalities, could you please explain what this means, the undefined parts of the six Sarajevo municipalities, in statistical terms.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Those are part that is have not been defined in statistical terms for the simple reason that there are no statistical limits reasons, statistically determined limits. There are probably certain political or military limits, data but not in statistical terms because there are certain areas that are determined, that are taken into consideration. In statistics there is a definite procedure according to which the statistical boundaries of an area are assessed, in terms of my field.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Radovanovic, you said that there was a procedure. If a statistician is carrying out an analysis, why is it necessary for these statistical areas to be determined?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, whenever a census is made, a census of the population or of households in particular, it's of great importance to define the statistical areas concerned by the census, and this is also important to avoid duplicating information or leaving out information. I can provide you with a detailed explanation of this. There is an elaborate procedure that is applied.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Radovanovic. On page 6, item 2 in the Serbian text - that's page 10 in the English version - you mention the shortcomings in Ewa Tabeau's findings. You say that she relies on the area where a census was carried out. You say that this included 88 municipalities. And my question would be: In those 89 local municipalities, do these 89 local municipalities represent a statistically defined area?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The municipalities -- the local communes weren't statistically or administratively defined. They were associations of citizens, associations that existed on a voluntary basis, and they would deal with certain utility problems or residential problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Radovanovic. You have explained to us what the idea of a local commune is in your report. Bearing in mind our time restrictions, I'll perhaps put a question of a general kind to you and could you briefly answer it. What is necessary in order to carry out a population census, a census of the population or a census of households?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, you need a lot of money. Census populations or household censuses, if you want to carry out a total -- a complete census, this costs a lot of money. In every state these are some of the most expensive actions that you can carry out in statistics. You intensify the preparations for three or four years before this. There is a very broad procedure and methodology that has to be used to prepare and carry out a census. This has to be done if you want the census to be carried out correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Radovanovic, when you mention methodology, what has to be precisely determined?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, you have to determine the exact area, you have to define the area that is concerned by the census, and then you have to determine what the objectives of the census are, you have to determine the units of the census, that is to say, what will be included in the census, and then it is necessary to determine the methodology which that will be used or, rather, the way in which you are going to proceed. And if you are carrying out such a wide statistical action, there are various kind of methodologies. There's an organisational methodology, how is it going to be organised, which organ will be concerned with certain fields, what does the statistical department do, what does the cadastral department do, and there is a methodology which refers to the instruments of the census. To simplify, the methodology is the way in which you are going to proceed, and everyone has to respect this procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Radovanovic, to the extent that I've understood your answers, you said that it was a state action within a framework of statistical methods. Are you aware of any census carried -- done by institutions that were not statistical institutions in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Or rather, if any such action was taken, all I can say is that it was never officially verified by official statistical institutes in the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Radovanovic, you mentioned censuses carried out by statistical institutes. If I've understood you, you said that methodology was important. And with reference to the methodology, you mentioned those carrying out the census. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. A census involves a large number of people. For example, the 1991 census in the territory of the former Yugoslavia involved over 100.000 people. Their tasks varied. Some people were involved in statistics and they have a certain number of tasks and then there are people who are not involved in statistics but similarly they are assigned certain tasks. Whenever a population census is being carried out, those carrying out the census out are the key people. There is a special procedure that concerns how those involved in the census are to be trained, et cetera. I apologise if that's of any importance. There were over 60.000 people involved in taking the census in the 1991 census. I can't say that that is the exact figure because it depended on the area of the republic. It varied from republic to republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Radovanovic, as far as I have understood your question, it's important for the person taking the census or the people taking the census to have certain qualifications. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. One of the conditions for carrying out a good census is to have people who are qualified. They have to have a certain level of literacy. They have to be of certain professional standards, because they have to be trained in order to master the methodology that has to be used when taking the census. The training that they are given provides them with a certain methodology that must be applied, that must be strictly applied if the census is to be valid, if it's to be carried out uniformly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If you're talking about the qualifications of those taking the census and the necessity of ensuring that the census is unified, it has certain uniformity, can you tell us what this means when you say it should have a certain uniformity.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Uniformity, that means that you have to strictly adhere to the methodology and you mustn't allow the census-taker to take decisions himself about certain factors because this is a huge project. It includes a lot of people, and you can't take decisions that do not conform. If you want valid information, then it is necessary to provide instructions as to how this is to be carried out. So the methodology has to be respected and this ensures a certain uniformity. The census-taker has to adhere to what is important for statistics. The census-taker is not free to assess independently what the information should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So Mrs. Radovanovic, you're telling us that the census-taker -- a census-taker can't be someone who is allowed to interpret the information provided to the census-taker when carrying out the census.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not allowed. There are penalties prescribed by the law. The census-taker has to strictly adhere to the methodology. But in statistics and especially in statistics that regard censuses, there are legal articles and there were many meetings that dealt with the subject of the influence excerpted by the census-taker. The census-taker can strictly adhere to a methodology but can nevertheless influence the results through his behaviour towards the subjects and by asking questions in an imprecise way. So in censuses it's been possible to detect the influence of the census-taker, especially in difficult times when the population is either not well informed or does not want to provide information because they fear certain things. I can provide you with an example that is interesting for economical reasons. For example, very often the population, especially those involved in agriculture, wanted to conceal the amount of land they possessed and the amount of cattle they possessed in order to avoid taxes. And if you have a census-taker who is not able to explain the reasons for which a census is being taken, then you get a totally -- you get -- the information you get about the cattle possessed is totally false.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Radovanovic, as someone who is involved in statistics, and we're now talking about censuses and the methodology used by census-takers, can you tell us what instruments, what tools are used when taking a census?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, above all the tools could be divided into the main and secondary tools. A large number of tools are involved. You have to determine the statistical areas with precision. I have to determine all the forms, all the instructions that accompany this, and one of the main tools, if we're talking about population censuses or household censuses, one of the main tools are questionnaires. For example, these are used for censuses and you have those methodological instructions. And regular censuses also have another important tool: That's a control method. You have to record what sort of statistics are involved in that control procedure. You have to try to avoid duplicating results, and you have strictly defined -- strictly defined boundaries, strictly defined areas in which the census-taker can move. For example, if it's defined as a street. And you say the census-taker of a certain area, 52, shall adhere to the left side of the Proletarski Brigada Street and shall deal with houses 52 to 56 to 180 and then crosses the road at the traffic lights and takes the census of the houses number 2 and 4 on the right-hand side of the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Radovanovic, I'd like to stop you there. Although you have answered my question, as one of the tools used in a census you mentioned, if I have understood your answer -- you mentioned questionnaires, and you said that that was the most important tool used in censuses. What should a questionnaire contain when used as a tool in a census?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, above all, a questionnaire has to be clear and the questions must be quite precisely defined, and it has to relate to the units that it is interested in.
